newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - History lessons.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - History lessons.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
One of the reasons that aviation insurance rates are falling (see "Aviation insurers remain glum on rates outlook") is the lack of a historical perspective on the part of newcomers to the market.
Claims have fallen sharply from a peak in 1994, encouraging those with short memories into the market.

However, insuring jet aircraft is very much catastrophe "all or nothing business". One accident involving an expensive new aircraft and passengers from countries where lawyers can push for high levels of death and injury compensation can plunge the whole industry into a loss.
Eleven Western built jets on passenger flights were involved in fatal accidents last year. However, the loss of just one, TWA flight 800, places a huge question mark over the entire 1996 account.
London-based airline insurers yesterday described current aviation premium rates as unsustainably low, arguing that they do not reflect the long terms ups and downs of air accident history.

London aviation underwriters say they tend to charge higher rates than elsewhere and have consequently been losing business. Other European countries, such as France, are proving particularly aggressive on price, they say.

The Lloyd's of London market is also playing its part in driving rates lower, company underwriters said. New corporate capital flowing into Lloyd's is willing to take on aviation business at very cheap rates simply to get a piece of the business.
Even the prospect of higher liability payouts once new rules come into force to replace the Warsaw Convention is unlikely to be enough to reverse the downward trend in rates.

Although new players are entering the market, the long term trend in aviation, as in other parts of the insurance industry, has been towards a gradual consolidation. Fewer, bigger units means lower costs and greater concentration on underwriting.
One year of heavy claims with rates so low could speed up the process of consolidation and weed out some of the newcomers.
